newsitem.title: UK: Sprinkle iron on the sea, stop global warming.
newsitem.headline: Sprinkle iron on the sea, stop global warming.

text.p: Fertilisation of the oceans with iron could cause a major reduction in global warming by triggering widespread "blooming" of carbon dioxide-consuming plankton, scientists said on Friday.
They said that if the whole of the Southern Ocean was treated with iron, carbon dioxide over that region could be lowered by up to 21 percent.
In an experiment by American and British scientists in 1995, dissolved iron was infused into the surface of a 60 sq km (23.2 sq mile) patch of water in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

Plankton, micro-organisms at the end of the food chain, are not abundant in the equatorial Pacific despite the availability of essential nutrients like nitrate and phosphate. Scientists had long thought low iron levels were to blame for the shortage.

Within a week of the iron sowing, a transformation described as "almost biblical" by one scientist had occurred as plankton bloomed, turning the ocean dark green. Although tiny, plankton are probably the biggest users of carbon dioxide on earth.

"The oceans are both a major source and sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide, and processes that control the balance of these fluxes are thought to have a major effect on global climate," scientists from Moss Landing Marine Laboratories in California said in one of four papers published in Nature magazine.
Global warming is due in part to a build-up of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from human activities such as burning fuel.
The scientists said the blooming of the plankton reduces carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere in two ways.

Plankton, because of better photosynthesis, sucked more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Over time it will sweep it down to the ocean floor. But plankton also produces dimethyl sulphide (DMS) as a waste product.
When oxidised to sulphate in the atmosphere, DMS produces particles which forms clouds shielding the earth from radiation.
"The phytoplankton are thus of vital importance in the regulation of the climate, and perhaps a brake on the greenhouse effect," Nature said in a press release.

The experiment differed from an earlier attempt in 1993 to enrich the Pacific with iron because the iron was added over several days, not just as one dose. The equatorial Pacific and the Southern Ocean are the largest low-plankton areas.

Speaking of the 1995 experiment, scientists from Plymouth Marine Laboraroty in south-west England said: "If the Southern Ocean can be similarly influenced, changes to iron supply there could lower the atmospheric CO2 concentration by six to 21 percent."

The stimulated production of plankton was, however, short-lived. Within a week of the last infusion, the plankton bloom had faded and there was no sign the iron was retained and efficiently recycled in the sea.
